notes.definition: Speciation is the formation of a new species. It happens when populations of one species become so different, usually after being isolated, that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
explanation: A species is a group of similar organisms that can breed together to produce fertile offspring. Sometimes two different species can mate, but their offspring are infertile. For example, a horse and a donkey can produce a mule, but mules cannot breed, so horses and donkeys are separate species. Speciation is the process that produces a new species, and it is the way that natural selection, acting over very long periods of time, leads to the huge diversity of species on Earth.

Alfred Russel Wallace was a naturalist who worked worldwide gathering evidence for evolutionary theory, collecting thousands of specimens in places such as the Amazon basin and the islands of Southeast Asia. He independently came up with the theory of evolution by natural selection at the same time as Charles Darwin. In 1858 Wallace and Darwin published joint writings on the theory. This prompted Darwin to publish his famous book, On the Origin of Species, the following year (1859).

Wallace is best known for two pieces of work. The first is his work on warning colouration in animals. Some animals, such as certain caterpillars, are brightly coloured and taste unpleasant or are poisonous. Predators learn to avoid them, so the bright colouration helps them survive and is favoured by natural selection. The second is his theory of speciation: he realised that new species arise when populations become separated and adapt to different conditions. Wallace did much pioneering work on speciation, but more evidence gathered over time has led to our current understanding of the theory.

Speciation happens in a series of steps. First, isolation: two populations of one species become separated, often by a geographical barrier such as a mountain range, a river, a stretch of sea or a desert, so they can no longer meet and breed. Second, genetic variation: each population contains a wide range of alleles, because mutations happen at random and sexual reproduction mixes alleles. Third, natural selection: the conditions on each side of the barrier are different (for example climate, food or predators), so different alleles give an advantage in each area.

In each population, individuals with the characteristics best suited to their own environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing on their advantageous alleles to their offspring. Over many generations the advantageous alleles become more common in each population, but different alleles are selected in each one. Eventually the two populations become so different that, even if the barrier were removed, individuals from the two populations could no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring. At this point they are two separate species and speciation has occurred.

Isolation is important because if the populations could still meet and breed, their alleles would keep mixing and the populations would not become different enough. Speciation usually takes a very long time, often thousands or millions of generations, so it is rarely seen directly in animals. Island species are a good illustration: Wallace and Darwin both noticed that species on islands were similar to, but different from, species on the nearest mainland, which suggested they had descended from mainland ancestors and changed after becoming isolated.

keyTerms.definition: A group of similar organisms that can breed together to produce fertile offspring.
The formation of a new species when populations become so different that they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
The separation of two populations of a species so that they cannot meet and breed, often by a geographical barrier.
A physical feature, such as a mountain range, river, sea or desert, that separates populations.
Differences in the alleles carried by individuals in a population, caused by mutation and sexual reproduction.

Offspring that are able to reproduce themselves.

workedExamples.title: Applying the steps of speciation to an unfamiliar example
workedExamples.question: A population of beetles lived in a forest. A wide new river formed, splitting the forest in two. The north side became cooler and wetter, and the south side became warmer and drier. Explain how two species of beetle could form.
steps: Isolation: the river is a geographical barrier, so beetles on the two sides cannot meet and interbreed.
Genetic variation: each population has a range of alleles because of mutations, so beetles vary, for example in how well they resist drying out.
Natural selection: on the dry south side, beetles with alleles that reduce water loss are more likely to survive and reproduce. On the wet north side, different alleles give an advantage.
Over many generations, the advantageous alleles become more common in each population, but they are different alleles in each population.
Eventually the two populations are so different that they cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring, even if they meet again.
workedExamples.answer: The river isolates the populations; mutations give variation; different conditions mean natural selection favours different alleles on each side; after many generations the populations can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring, so they are two species.

workedExamples.title: Deciding whether two populations are separate species
workedExamples.question: Lions and tigers can breed in zoos to produce ligers. Male ligers are infertile. Are lions and tigers the same species? Explain your answer.
steps: Recall the definition: a species is a group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
Lions and tigers can mate, but the male offspring are infertile.
Producing offspring is not enough: the offspring must be fertile for the parents to be the same species.
workedExamples.answer: No. Lions and tigers are separate species because their offspring are not (reliably) fertile.

workedExamples.title: Putting the Darwin and Wallace events in order
workedExamples.question: Put these events in order: Darwin publishes On the Origin of Species; Wallace develops the theory of natural selection independently while collecting specimens; Darwin and Wallace publish joint writings.
steps: Wallace worked out his ideas while gathering evidence abroad and sent them to Darwin.
In 1858 their ideas were published together as joint writings.
This prompted Darwin to publish On the Origin of Species the following year, 1859.
workedExamples.answer: Wallace develops the theory independently; joint writings published (1858); On the Origin of Species published (1859).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think that any two animals that can mate must be the same species.
misconceptions.right: In fact, to be the same species they must be able to produce fertile offspring. Horses and donkeys produce infertile mules, so they are different species.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the geographical barrier itself causes the changes, for example that a river makes the animals mutate.
misconceptions.right: In fact, the barrier only stops interbreeding. Mutations happen at random, and the different conditions on each side mean natural selection favours different alleles.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think individuals change during their lifetime to suit their new environment and then pass this on.
misconceptions.right: In fact, individuals do not choose to change. Individuals that already have advantageous alleles are more likely to survive and reproduce, so those alleles become more common over many generations.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think Darwin came up with natural selection entirely on his own.
misconceptions.right: In fact, Wallace independently proposed the same theory, and their joint writings in 1858 prompted Darwin to publish On the Origin of Species in 1859.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think speciation happens in one or two generations.
misconceptions.right: In fact, speciation usually takes many generations, often thousands of years or more.

realWorld: Island species, such as the many different species of finches and tortoises on the Galápagos Islands, are similar to mainland species but have changed after becoming isolated.
Conservationists consider whether populations are separate species when deciding which populations need protecting.
Warning colouration studied by Wallace is seen in wasps, poison dart frogs and ladybirds, and is copied in the bright colours of warning signs.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic is in separate Biology only (not Combined Science Trilogy): the work of Alfred Russel Wallace, his joint writings with Darwin (1858), warning colouration, and the steps that give rise to new species (isolation, genetic variation, natural selection, inability to interbreed to produce fertile offspring).
examTips: Learn the four steps of speciation in order: isolation, genetic variation, natural selection, can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring. Use these words in long answers.
Always say 'fertile offspring' when defining a species. Just saying 'can breed' will not get the mark.
In speciation answers, say that conditions are different on each side of the barrier, so different alleles are selected for in each population.
Mention 'over many generations' to show you understand that speciation is slow.
Remember the dates: joint writings 1858, On the Origin of Species 1859.

questions.question: Which statement best describes a species?
options: A group of organisms that live in the same habitat
A group of similar organisms that can breed together to produce fertile offspring
A group of organisms that share the same genus name
A group of organisms that look identical
markScheme: 1 mark: a group of similar organisms that can breed together to produce fertile offspring
questions.explanation: The key test for a species is producing fertile offspring. Organisms in one habitat may be many different species, organisms in the same genus can be different species, and members of a species are often not identical.

questions.question: Which scientist independently proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection at the same time as Charles Darwin?
options: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck
Gregor Mendel
Alfred Russel Wallace
Carl Linnaeus
markScheme: 1 mark: Alfred Russel Wallace
questions.explanation: Wallace came up with natural selection independently. Lamarck proposed the inheritance of acquired characteristics, Mendel studied inheritance in pea plants and Linnaeus developed a classification system.

questions.question: In which year did Darwin and Wallace publish joint writings on evolution by natural selection?
markScheme: 1 mark: 1858
questions.explanation: The joint writings were published in 1858. On the Origin of Species followed in 1859, so 1859 is a common wrong answer.

questions.question: What is usually the first step in the formation of a new species?
options: Two populations become isolated from each other
The populations can no longer interbreed
Natural selection favours different alleles
Every individual in the population mutates
markScheme: 1 mark: two populations become isolated
questions.explanation: Speciation starts with isolation, for example by a geographical barrier. Natural selection then acts in each population and, at the end, they can no longer interbreed. Mutations are random and only affect individuals.

questions.question: Alfred Russel Wallace is best known for which two pieces of work?
options: Breeding experiments on pea plants and the idea of inherited units
The binomial naming system and the classification of plants
The structure of DNA and how genes work
Warning colouration in animals and his theory of speciation
markScheme: 1 mark: warning colouration in animals and his theory of speciation
questions.explanation: Wallace is best known for warning colouration and speciation. Pea breeding was Mendel, binomial naming was Linnaeus, and the structure of DNA was worked out in the mid-20th century.

questions.question: Which observation would show that two populations of birds have become separate species?
options: The birds in the two populations have different coloured feathers
The two populations live on different islands
Birds from the two populations cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring
The two populations eat different types of seed
markScheme: 1 mark: cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring
questions.explanation: Appearance, location and diet can all differ within one species. Only the inability to produce fertile offspring shows that they are separate species.

questions.question: A horse and a donkey can mate to produce a mule. Mules are infertile. What does this show?
options: Horses and donkeys are the same species because they can mate
Horses and donkeys are different species because their offspring are infertile
Mules are a new species formed by speciation
Mules are infertile because they have no genetic variation
markScheme: 1 mark: horses and donkeys are different species because their offspring are infertile
questions.explanation: Being able to mate is not enough; members of a species produce fertile offspring. Mules cannot breed, so they are not a new species, and their infertility is not due to a lack of variation.

questions.question: Which of these could act as a geographical barrier that isolates two populations?
options: A mountain range
A difference in fur colour
A random mutation
A change in diet
markScheme: 1 mark: a mountain range
questions.explanation: A geographical barrier is a physical feature such as a mountain range, river, sea or desert. Fur colour, mutations and diet are not physical features that separate populations.

questions.question: Why is genetic variation within each population needed for speciation?
options: It makes sure every individual survives
It stops the populations from becoming isolated
It makes all individuals in a population identical
It provides different alleles for natural selection to act on
markScheme: 1 mark: it provides different alleles for natural selection to act on
questions.explanation: Without variation there would be nothing for natural selection to choose between. Variation does not guarantee survival, does not affect isolation and makes individuals different, not identical.

questions.question: Two populations of one species of snail are separated by a river. Which statement best explains why they become more and more different over time?
options: Snails on each side change during their lifetime to suit their surroundings and pass these changes on
The river causes the same mutations in both populations
Conditions differ on each side, so natural selection favours different alleles in each population
The snails on each side choose not to mate with each other
markScheme: 1 mark: conditions differ on each side, so natural selection favours different alleles in each population
questions.explanation: The first option describes the inheritance of acquired characteristics (Lamarck), which is wrong. The river does not cause mutations; mutations are random. Isolation stops mating because the snails cannot meet, not because they choose not to.

questions.question: In which situation is speciation least likely to happen?
options: A population of lizards is split between two islands far apart with different climates
A population of fish is split into two lakes, one with clear water and one with muddy water
A population of mice lives in a wood where a small stream is easily crossed every day
A population of plants is split by a new mountain range, with one side much wetter than the other
markScheme: 1 mark: the mice crossing the small stream
questions.explanation: If individuals can still cross the stream and interbreed, alleles keep mixing between the two groups, so they do not become different enough to form new species. In the other examples the populations are isolated and face different conditions.

questions.question: Give the title of the book that Darwin published in 1859.
markScheme: 1 mark: On the Origin of Species
questions.explanation: Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, the year after the joint writings with Wallace.

questions.question: Give two examples of geographical barriers that could isolate two populations of a species.
markScheme: 1 mark: first correct barrier (e.g. mountain range)
1 mark: second correct barrier (e.g. river, sea, desert)
questions.explanation: Any physical feature that stops individuals meeting and interbreeding is a geographical barrier. Mountains, rivers, seas and deserts are the most common examples.

questions.question: What is meant by speciation?
markScheme: 1 mark: the formation of a new species
1 mark: when populations become so different they can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring
questions.explanation: Speciation is the formation of a new species. The second mark needs the idea that the populations can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

questions.question: Name the process in which individuals with characteristics best suited to their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce.
markScheme: 1 mark: natural selection
questions.explanation: This is natural selection. It is the third step of speciation, acting differently in each isolated population.

questions.question: Some caterpillars that taste unpleasant to birds are brightly coloured. Wallace studied this warning colouration. Explain how the bright colouration helps the caterpillars survive.
markScheme: 1 mark: the bright colours warn predators / birds that the caterpillar tastes unpleasant or is poisonous
1 mark: so predators learn to avoid them and they are less likely to be eaten
questions.explanation: Predators that try one bright, bad-tasting caterpillar learn to avoid others like it. Brightly coloured caterpillars are therefore more likely to survive and reproduce, so the colouration is favoured by natural selection.

questions.question: Describe how the joint writings of Darwin and Wallace in 1858 affected Darwin's work.
markScheme: 1 mark: they prompted Darwin to publish his book On the Origin of Species
1 mark: the following year / in 1859
questions.explanation: Darwin had been developing his ideas for many years but had not published them. Wallace's independent work and their joint writings in 1858 prompted Darwin to publish On the Origin of Species in 1859.

questions.question: Explain why mutations are important for speciation.
markScheme: 1 mark: mutations produce new alleles / genetic variation
1 mark: some alleles give an advantage so they can be selected for by natural selection
questions.explanation: Mutations are the source of new alleles. Without this variation, natural selection could not make the two isolated populations different from each other.

questions.question: Explain why two populations must usually be isolated from each other for speciation to happen.
markScheme: 1 mark: isolation stops the populations meeting and interbreeding
1 mark: otherwise alleles keep mixing between them so they do not become different enough to form separate species
questions.explanation: If the two groups could still breed together, any differences selected in one group would be mixed into the other. Isolation lets each population change independently.

questions.question: Wallace worked worldwide gathering evidence for evolutionary theory. Suggest why studying animals on many different islands was useful evidence for his theory of speciation.
markScheme: 1 mark: island populations are isolated (by sea) from other populations
1 mark: species on islands are similar to, but different from, species elsewhere / on the mainland, suggesting they changed after becoming isolated
questions.explanation: Islands are natural experiments in isolation. Finding related but different species on nearby islands suggests that one ancestral species became separated and changed in different ways.

questions.question:
Two populations of mice were separated by a river for many thousands of years. The river then dried up. Mice from the two populations mated, but all their offspring were infertile.
Explain whether the two populations are still the same species, and suggest why this has happened.
markScheme: 1 mark: they are now different species
1 mark: because they cannot produce fertile offspring
1 mark: because during isolation natural selection favoured different alleles in each population, so they became too different
questions.explanation: Mating alone does not make two groups the same species. The offspring are infertile, so speciation has happened. While isolated, each population adapted to its own conditions over many generations.

questions.question: Wallace did much pioneering work on speciation, but our current understanding of speciation is different from his. Suggest why our understanding has changed.
markScheme: 1 mark: more evidence has been collected over time
1 mark: e.g. genes, alleles, mutations and DNA were not known in Wallace's time, so the genetic basis of variation can now be explained
questions.explanation: Scientific theories develop as new evidence appears. Wallace did not know about genes or DNA, so he could not explain where variation came from or how characteristics were inherited.

questions.question: A plant species grows on both sides of a newly formed mountain range. Over many years, the west side becomes much wetter than the east side. Explain why the plants on the east side might evolve to have smaller leaves with thicker waxy layers.
markScheme: 1 mark: there is variation in leaf size / wax thickness (due to mutation)
1 mark: on the drier east side, plants with smaller, waxier leaves lose less water so are more likely to survive and reproduce
1 mark: they pass on these alleles, so over many generations these alleles become more common
questions.explanation: This is natural selection in one isolated population. The alleles for smaller, waxier leaves already exist through mutation; they become common because of the dry conditions, not because the plants try to change.

questions.question: A student says: 'A geographical barrier causes speciation because it makes the animals mutate.' Evaluate this statement.
markScheme: 1 mark: the statement is wrong because mutations happen at random / are not caused by the barrier
1 mark: the barrier isolates the populations / stops interbreeding, and different conditions mean natural selection favours different alleles
questions.explanation: The barrier's role is to stop interbreeding. The changes come from random mutation followed by natural selection in different conditions on each side.

questions.question: Describe the work of Alfred Russel Wallace and how it contributed to the theory of evolution by natural selection.
markScheme: Indicative content: Wallace worked worldwide gathering evidence for evolution (collected specimens, e.g. in South America and Southeast Asia); he independently proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection; he published joint writings with Darwin in 1858; this prompted Darwin to publish On the Origin of Species in 1859; he is best known for work on warning colouration in animals (bright colours warn predators of unpleasant taste); he developed a theory of speciation; his pioneering work on speciation has since been developed with more evidence.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear description of several aspects of Wallace's work, linked to how it contributed to the theory (e.g. joint writings prompting Darwin to publish).
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about Wallace's work with little linking.
questions.explanation: Strong answers mention both the independent discovery of natural selection with the 1858 joint writings and the 1859 book, and the two things Wallace is best known for: warning colouration and speciation.

questions.question: Compare the contributions of Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace to the theory of evolution by natural selection.
markScheme: Indicative content. Similarities: both proposed the theory of evolution by natural selection independently; both gathered evidence from observing organisms (including on islands); they published joint writings in 1858. Differences: Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859 (prompted by Wallace's work), which set out the theory in detail with lots of evidence; Wallace is best known for work on warning colouration and his theory of speciation; Wallace worked worldwide collecting specimens.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least one clear similarity and one clear difference, with accurate detail.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): facts about one or both scientists, with little direct comparison.
questions.explanation: A compare question needs similarities and differences, ideally using linking words such as 'both' and 'whereas'. Facts about only one scientist cannot reach the top level.

questions.question:
A population of lizards lived on the mainland. During a storm, some lizards were carried on floating vegetation to a distant island. The island has different food plants and a hotter, drier climate than the mainland.
Explain how a new species of lizard could form on the island.
markScheme: Indicative content: the island population is isolated from the mainland population by the sea (geographical barrier); the two populations cannot interbreed; there is genetic variation in each population due to mutations (and sexual reproduction); conditions on the island are different (hotter, drier, different food); natural selection: individuals with characteristics best suited to island conditions (e.g. better at reducing water loss, jaws suited to the island food plants) are more likely to survive and reproduce; they pass on their advantageous alleles to their offspring; on the mainland different alleles are selected for; over many generations the allele frequencies / characteristics in the two populations become very different; eventually the populations can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring; so they are separate species.

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, logically sequenced explanation including isolation, variation from mutation, natural selection of advantageous alleles in different conditions over many generations, and the end point of being unable to interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): an explanation with most steps but some gaps, for example no mention of mutation or fertile offspring.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as 'they became different' or 'they adapted', with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Use the four steps as a framework and apply them to the context: sea as the barrier, the hot dry climate and new food as the different conditions, and 'cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring' as the end point.

questions.question:
A large lake contained one species of fish. Over thousands of years the water level fell and the lake split into two lakes. Lake A is deep with clear water and many large predatory birds. Lake B is shallow and muddy with few predators but little food.
Today the fish in the two lakes cannot interbreed to produce fertile offspring. Explain how this situation arose and why scientists now classify the fish as two species.
markScheme: Indicative content: the fall in water level isolated the two fish populations; they could not interbreed; each population had genetic variation from mutations; the conditions differed: predation pressure in lake A, food shortage in lake B; in lake A, fish with characteristics that help them avoid predators (e.g. camouflage, faster swimming) were more likely to survive and reproduce; in lake B, fish best able to find or use limited food (e.g. smaller size, feeding in mud) were more likely to survive and reproduce; advantageous alleles were passed on and became more common in each lake; different alleles were selected in each lake; over many generations the populations became very different; they are classified as two species because a species is a group that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring, and these fish no longer can.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed and coherent explanation linking isolation, variation, different selection pressures in each lake and the species definition.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a reasonable explanation with some links, for example natural selection described for one lake only, or species definition missing.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): basic points about the lakes being separate or fish adapting, with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Top answers apply natural selection separately to both lakes, giving a suitable advantageous characteristic for each, and finish by using the definition of a species to justify the classification.
